title: The fire-then-flood cycle in LA's hills
text: In Los Angeles, fire and flood are linked. Santa Ana winds in fall and winter push fires through dry chaparral, as in January 2025 when the Palisades and Eaton fires burned 59 square miles. The burned slopes then shed water instead of soaking it up, so the next rains bring mud and debris flows. The NWS notes a debris flow can start after only a few minutes of intense rain. In February 2025 a debris flow swept an LAFD vehicle off Pacific Coast Highway; in February 2026 mud closed Topanga Canyon Boulevard again. County Public Works clears debris basins before storms, and burn-scar neighborhoods get evacuation warnings when heavy rain is forecast. Sources: FireRescue1; CBS Los Angeles; FOX Weather; Malibu Times.

title: LA's shrinking beaches
text: Some of LA County's most popular beaches are losing sand. Zuma narrowed by an average of 3.5 feet and Point Dume by about 40 feet between 2002 and 2022, and a USGS-led study ranks Zuma among the worst sand losers in California. In August 2026 erosion closed the Point Dume parking lot and Westward Beach Road, and in October 2026 surf flooded Zuma and forced emergency repairs. The County is responding with a program to reuse surplus construction sand at five beaches and with planning grants for a Zuma living shoreline and Dockweiler dunes, while state guidance expects about 0.8 feet of sea level rise by 2050. Sources: LA Public Press; Radio Malibu; NBC Los Angeles; DredgeWire; California Ocean Protection Council.

title: LA's climate and microclimates in brief
text: Los Angeles has a dry, mild Mediterranean-type climate. Downtown averages highs of 68 F in January and 84 F in August, with 14.25 inches of rain a year (1991-2020), nearly all from November to March. Distance from the ocean matters most: the coast stays mild under the marine layer, while the San Fernando Valley bakes; Woodland Hills set the county record of 121 F in 2020. Rainfall swings widely from year to year, and the long-term normal has drifted lower. Mountains on three sides trap pollution, giving the region the worst ozone in the country. Sources: NWS Los Angeles/Oxnard; ABC7; Sierra Photography weather notes; American Lung Association.

title: Mountains to the sea: the shape of Los Angeles
text: The City of Los Angeles runs from sea level at Venice and San Pedro to 5,075 feet at Mount Lukens, the largest high-to-low range of any of the 50 most populous US cities. The Santa Monica Mountains split the city between the coastal basin and the San Fernando Valley; the steep San Gabriel Mountains, topped by Mount Baldy at 10,064 feet, wall it off to the north, with the San Andreas Fault on their far side. The LA River runs 51 miles from Canoga Park to Long Beach, 32 of them in the city. Beneath it all, faults such as the Puente Hills thrust run under Downtown. Sources: Wikipedia (Mount Lukens; San Gabriel Mountains); LA County Public Works; California Earthquake Authority.

title: Current conditions: late October 2026
text: As of late October 2026, the region is at the start of its rainy season after a wet 2025-26 winter. title: Los Angeles River (river)
text: Los Angeles River is a river (City of LA (first 32 miles) and 13 other cities to Long Beach). Length: about 82 km (51 mi). Managed by Los Angeles County Public Works (Flood Control District). The LA River runs 51 miles from Canoga Park to Long Beach; the first 32 miles are in the City of LA. Its 834-square-mile watershed drains steep terrain over 7,000 feet high, so water rises quickly. After deadly floods in 1914, 1934 and 1938 it was lined in concrete by the Army Corps; a few soft-bottom stretches remain, such as the Glendale Narrows. Water in the channel can rise suddenly even on a sunny day. Hazards: River and urban flooding; Drought and rainfall swings. Key facts: channel capacity 129,000 cfs (full stage); corps maintained channel 22 miles (as of 2016-10-19); glendale narrows soft bottom 6.43 miles (as of 2016-10-19); length 51 miles (as of 2026-10-30); watershed area 834 sq mi (as of 2026-10-30). title: Hazard: Wildfire (wildland-urban interface)
text: Wildfire (wildland-urban interface) (fire hazard) in the Los Angeles area. Wind-driven brush fires are the defining hazard of LA's hills. About 900,000 acres of Greater LA are now mapped in state "very high" fire hazard zones. In January 2025 the Palisades and Eaton fires, driven by gusts forecast near 90 mph, burned 59 square miles, killed 31 people and destroyed 16,246 structures. Season: Year-round, worst in fall and winter when Santa Ana winds blow over dry brush. Drivers: Dry chaparral, low humidity, heat and strong offshore winds; ignitions near homes in the hills. Warning signals: NWS Red Flag Warnings; Santa Ana wind forecasts; humidity below about 15%; long dry spells. Typical impacts: Evacuations, destroyed homes, deaths, smoke, power shutoffs, burn scars that later produce debris flows. Most exposed places: Angeles National Forest (very high); San Gabriel Mountains (very high); Santa Monica Mountains (very high); Griffith Park (natural area) (high); San Fernando Valley (moderate). Responsible bodies: California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection (respond); California Governor's Office of Emergency Services (coordinate); Federal Emergency Management Agency (fund); Los Angeles County Fire Department (respond); Los Angeles Fire Department (respond); National Weather Service, Los Angeles/Oxnard (warn); US Forest Service: Angeles National Forest (respond). Sources: ABC7 Los Angeles; Wikipedia; Wikipedia (via Wikiwand); Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning; NBC Los Angeles.

title: Hazard: Santa Ana winds
text: Santa Ana winds (atmospheric hazard) in the Los Angeles area. Offshore Santa Ana winds turn small fires into fast-moving firestorms. In the first Santa Ana event of fall 2026 (Oct 15-18), gusts of 40-60 mph were widespread, 50-70 mph below passes and canyons, and peaked at 83 mph at Magic Mountain. Season: October through March, often strongest in late fall and winter. Drivers: High pressure over the Great Basin pushing hot, very dry air down through mountain passes and canyons toward the coast. Warning signals: NWS high wind warnings and Red Flag Warnings; low humidity; gusts below passes and canyons. Typical impacts: Rapid fire spread, downed trees and power lines, utility power shutoffs, extreme fire behavior. Most exposed places: San Gabriel Mountains (very high); San Fernando Valley (high); Santa Monica Mountains (high). Responsible bodies: Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (mitigate); National Weather Service, Los Angeles/Oxnard (warn). Sources: The Weather Channel; NBC Los Angeles.

title: Hazard: Post-fire mud and debris flows
text: Post-fire mud and debris flows (water hazard) in the Los Angeles area. Burn scars from the 2025 fires above Pacific Palisades, Malibu, Topanga, Altadena and Sierra Madre shed mud in heavy rain. According to the NWS, a debris flow does not need long rain or a saturated slope and can start after a few minutes of intense rain. In February 2025 a debris flow swept an LAFD vehicle off Pacific Coast Highway into the ocean. Season: Rainy season (November-March), for several years after a fire. Drivers: Intense bursts of rain on recently burned, water-repellent slopes. Warning signals: NWS flood and debris-flow watches; forecast rain rates of a quarter inch to an inch per hour over burn scars; evacuation warnings for burn-scar zones. Typical impacts: Mud and boulders burying roads and homes, vehicles swept away, road closures on PCH and Topanga, contaminated runoff onto beaches. Most exposed places: Eaton Fire burn scar (very high); Palisades Fire burn scar (very high); Topanga Canyon (SR 27) (very high); Will Rogers State Beach (moderate). Responsible bodies: Los Angeles County Public Works (Flood Control District) (mitigate); Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department (evacuate); Los Angeles Fire Department (evacuate); National Weather Service, Los Angeles/Oxnard (warn); US Geological Survey (assess). Sources: Malibu Times; CBS Los Angeles; Yahoo News / Los Angeles Times.

title: Hazard: River and urban flooding
text: River and urban flooding (water hazard) in the Los Angeles area. The LA River's 834-square-mile watershed drains terrain above 7,000 feet, so water rises fast. Deadly floods in 1914, 1934 and 1938 led to the concrete channel system, which now carries up to about 129,000 cubic feet per second. Season: Winter storms, especially atmospheric rivers (December-March). Drivers: Heavy, prolonged rain on steep mountain watersheds that drain quickly into concrete channels; paved urban surfaces. Warning signals: NWS flood watches and warnings; rapidly rising water in the LA River and other channels. Typical impacts: Swift water in channels, street flooding, people swept away in channels, bridge and road damage. Most exposed places: Los Angeles River (high); Ballona Creek (moderate); Malibu Creek (moderate); San Gabriel River (moderate). title: Hazard: Landslides and rockslides
text: Landslides and rockslides (geologic hazard) in the Los Angeles area. Landslides range from sudden rockslides, like the one that closed Topanga Canyon Boulevard for three months in 2024, to slow giant slides such as the Portuguese Bend complex on the Palos Verdes Peninsula, which wet winters accelerated to unprecedented speeds. title: Hazard: Beach and coastal erosion
text: Beach and coastal erosion (coastal hazard) in the Los Angeles area. Several LA County beaches are shrinking. Zuma narrowed by an average of 3.5 feet and Point Dume by 40 feet from 2002 to 2022. In 2025 the County approved a program to bring surplus sand from construction projects to Zuma, Will Rogers, Dockweiler, Manhattan and Redondo beaches. Drivers: Big waves at high tide, less sand reaching beaches from rivers, seawalls and roads that block natural movement, rising seas. title: Hazard: Sea level rise
text: Sea level rise (coastal hazard) in the Los Angeles area. California's 2024 guidance expects about 0.8 feet of sea level rise statewide by 2050 and 1.6 to 3.1 feet by 2100, with higher amounts possible. Combined with storms and high tides, this worsens flooding and erosion on LA's narrow beaches. Season: Gradual, with storm and high-tide peaks. Drivers: Ocean warming and melting land ice. Warning signals: State planning scenarios; flooding during king tides and storms. Typical impacts: More frequent coastal flooding, faster erosion, rising groundwater near the coast. title: Hazard: Earthquakes
text: Earthquakes (geologic hazard) in the Los Angeles area. The LA region sits on a dense network of faults that can rupture together. UCERF3, as summarized by EarthquakeTracker, puts the chance of a magnitude 6.7 or larger quake within 100 km of LA in the next 30 years at about 60%. The 1994 Northridge earthquake (M6.7) killed about 57 people and caused $13-50 billion in damage. Season: Any time. Drivers: Movement on the San Andreas and many local faults, including blind thrusts under the basin. Warning signals: None reliable in advance; early-warning alerts give seconds of notice. Typical impacts: Collapsed buildings and freeways, fires, landslides, broken water and gas lines. Most exposed places: Puente Hills Thrust Fault (very high); San Andreas Fault (southern section) (very high); Newport-Inglewood Fault (high); San Fernando Valley (high). title: Hazard: Extreme heat
text: Extreme heat (atmospheric hazard) in the Los Angeles area. Heat is uneven: in Downtown LA the average August high is 84 F, but inland valleys are much hotter. Woodland Hills hit 121 F on Sept 6, 2020, LA County's highest official temperature, while Downtown reached 111 F. Season: June through October; September heat waves are common. Drivers: High pressure, offshore flow, distance from the ocean (valleys are far hotter than the coast). Warning signals: NWS heat advisories and excessive heat warnings. Typical impacts: Heat illness and deaths, power grid strain, worse air quality and fire risk. Most exposed places: San Fernando Valley (very high); Los Angeles Basin (coastal plain) (moderate). title: Hazard: Smog and air pollution
text: Smog and air pollution (atmospheric hazard) in the Los Angeles area. The LA-Long Beach area ranked worst in the nation for ozone in the 2026 State of the Air report, for the 26th time in 27 reports, and 7th worst for short-term particle pollution. Season: Ozone worst in summer heat; particle pollution spikes with wildfire smoke and winter inversions. Drivers: Vehicle and industrial emissions cooked by sunshine and trapped by surrounding mountains and temperature inversions. Warning signals: AQMD and AirNow alerts; smoke advisories during fires. Typical impacts: Asthma and respiratory illness, especially in children. Most exposed places: Los Angeles Basin (coastal plain) (very high); San Fernando Valley (high). Responsible bodies: Los Angeles County Department of Public Health (warn); South Coast Air Quality Management District (regulate). Sources: American Lung Association; Spectrum News.

title: Hazard: Drought and rainfall swings
text: Drought and rainfall swings (water hazard) in the Los Angeles area. LA's rainfall swings from very dry to very wet years. The Downtown normal fell from 15.14 inches (1971-2000) to 14.25 inches (1991-2020). The 2025-26 water year was wet, with 18.36 inches by late February 2026. Season: Multi-year; rain falls almost entirely November to March. Drivers: Highly variable winter storms; warming temperatures; long dry spells. Warning signals: Below-normal rainfall to date; dry brush; drought monitor categories. Typical impacts: Water restrictions, dry fuels that feed wildfires, stressed vegetation. Most exposed places: Angeles National Forest (high); Los Angeles River (moderate). Responsible bodies: Governor of California (declare); Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (manage). Sources: Sierra Photography weather notes; Los Angeles County Public Works; Los Angeles County Department of Regional Planning.
